exercises.statement: In a company with a unitary (one-tier) board, what is the main role of a non-executive director?
options: To run a business division on a day-to-day basis.
To audit the financial statements and sign the audit report.
To represent employees in collective bargaining.
To oversee and constructively challenge management without being involved in day-to-day operations.
exercises.explanation: Option 4 is correct: non-executive directors (NEDs) sit on the board but are not part of the management team; they monitor performance, challenge strategy and often serve on board committees. Option 1 describes an executive director or a senior manager. Option 2 is the role of the external (statutory) auditor, who is independent from the board. Option 3 is the role of trade unions or employee representatives, not of NEDs.
exercises.source_ref: UK Corporate Governance Code (FRC), section 2 "Division of responsibilities" — role of non-executive directors

exercises.statement: Under the EU Audit Directive (Directive 2006/43/EC, art. 39, as amended), which of the following are tasks of the audit committee of a public-interest entity? Select all that apply.
options: Monitoring the effectiveness of the company's internal quality control and risk management systems.
Preparing the annual financial statements in place of the finance department.
Reviewing and monitoring the independence of the statutory auditor.
Setting the remuneration of executive directors.
exercises.explanation: Options 1 and 3 are correct: art. 39 lists, among others, informing the board of the outcome of the audit, monitoring the financial reporting process, monitoring the effectiveness of internal quality control and risk management systems, monitoring the statutory audit, reviewing and monitoring the independence of the auditor, and being responsible for the auditor selection procedure. Option 2 is wrong: management prepares the financial statements; the committee oversees the process, it does not replace the preparers. Option 4 is the task of the remuneration committee (and of the board), not of the audit committee.
exercises.source_ref: Directive 2006/43/EC, art. 39(6), as amended by Directive 2014/56/EU

exercises.statement: The Shareholder Rights Directive II (Directive (EU) 2017/828) requires listed companies to give shareholders a vote on the directors' remuneration policy, but leaves member states free to make that vote binding or advisory.
exercises.justification: True: SRD II introduced a vote on the remuneration policy and on the remuneration report; member states may provide that the policy vote is advisory rather than binding.
exercises.explanation: SRD II (art. 9a and 9b inserted into Directive 2007/36/EC) organises "say on pay" in two parts: an ex ante vote on the remuneration policy, at least every four years and at each material change, and a vote on the remuneration report describing pay actually awarded. The policy vote is binding by default, but member states may make it advisory; the report vote is in principle advisory. France chose a binding policy vote for listed companies and added ex post votes: the payment of variable and exceptional pay to each executive officer is conditional on shareholder approval.
exercises.source_ref: Directive (EU) 2017/828 (SRD II), inserting art. 9a (remuneration policy) and 9b (remuneration report) into Directive 2007/36/EC

exercises.title: An activist investor at Harbourline plc

sub_questions.prompt: Calculate Harbourline's dividend payout ratio for last year, in %.
If Harbourline had applied the 60% payout ratio demanded by Crestview to last year's net income, how much additional cash (in €m) would it have distributed compared with the dividends actually paid?
What is the usual name for Crestview's strategy of submitting its own resolutions and soliciting other shareholders' votes at the AGM?
sub_questions.explanation: A proxy fight (or proxy contest) is a campaign to win shareholders' votes, often by collecting their proxies, against the board's position. A squeeze-out is the compulsory buy-out of remaining minority shareholders after a takeover; a poison pill is a takeover defence; a rights issue is a share issue offered to existing shareholders.

sub_questions.prompt: In English, assess the governance arguments raised by Crestview and recommend how the board should respond.
sub_questions.model_answer: Crestview's governance arguments have merit. With only three independent directors out of nine and a founder who is both chair and CEO, oversight of management is weak: most governance codes recommend that at least half the board (excluding the chair) be independent and that the roles of chair and CEO be separated, or that a senior or lead independent director be appointed if they are combined (under "comply or explain"). The capital allocation argument is more debatable: a 25% payout ratio and €150m of net cash may indicate excess capital, but the board should assess the group's investment needs (fleet, warehouses, acquisitions) before committing to a 60% payout; a share buyback or a special dividend could return surplus cash more flexibly. The board should engage with Crestview and the other major shareholders rather than simply reject the proposals, explain its capital allocation policy clearly, strengthen board independence (for example by appointing new independent directors selected through the nomination committee, not necessarily Crestview's candidates) and consider appointing a lead independent director. A transparent response reduces the risk of losing the AGM votes.
key_points: Weak independence (3 out of 9) and combined chair/CEO roles: legitimate governance concerns under codes and comply or explain
Capital allocation: net cash and low payout, but the board must weigh investment needs; buyback or special dividend as flexible alternatives
Engage with the activist and other shareholders rather than reject outright
Strengthen independence via the nomination committee, lead independent director

exercises.explanation: The payout ratio (dividends / net income) is 25%; a 60% payout on €80m would mean €48m of dividends, i.e. €28m more. The case illustrates shareholder activism (public letter, proxy fight), board independence, the separation of chair and CEO roles and the "comply or explain" principle.
exercises.source_ref: UK Corporate Governance Code (FRC), provisions on board independence and separation of chair and CEO roles ; Afep-Medef Code, independent directors ; payout ratio = dividends / net income

exercises.statement: The board of a French listed company applying the Afep-Medef Code reviews the independence of four non-executive directors. Which director can be qualified as independent under the Code's criteria?
options: A university professor who joined the board four years ago, holds 2,000 shares of the company and receives only directors' fees.
A former deputy CEO of the group who left his executive position three years ago.
A retired audit partner who, until two years ago, signed the company's accounts as its statutory auditor.
A director who has sat on the board for thirteen years and has never held an executive position in the group.
exercises.explanation: Option 1 meets the criteria: no executive or employee role, no business relationship, a tenure of four years, and holding a small number of shares is even encouraged by governance codes; directors' fees do not impair independence. Option 2 fails the cooling-off criterion: no employee or executive position in the company or its group in the previous five years. Option 3 fails the criterion excluding anyone who has been the company's statutory auditor in the previous five years. Option 4 fails the tenure criterion: a director loses independent status once his or her term exceeds twelve years. Non-executive does not mean independent.
exercises.source_ref: Afep-Medef Corporate Governance Code (December 2022 version, still current in 2026), §10.5, criteria for assessing directors' independence (employee or executive in the previous five years, statutory auditor in the previous five years, more than twelve years on the board)

exercises.front: In executive pay, what is the difference between "malus" and "clawback"?
exercises.back:
Malus: the reduction or cancellation of variable pay (bonus, performance shares) before it vests or is paid, e.g. after misconduct or a material misstatement.
Clawback: the recovery of variable pay that has already been paid or has vested.
Both are usually set out in the remuneration policy submitted to shareholders.
French: clause de malus / clause de restitution (clawback).
exercises.explanation: Malus is easier to apply because the money has not yet been paid; clawback requires the company to recover sums from the executive, which may need legal action. The UK Corporate Governance Code (2024) expects directors' contracts and remuneration documents to include malus and clawback provisions (provision 37) and the annual report to describe them and state whether they were used during the year (provision 38).
exercises.source_ref: UK Corporate Governance Code (FRC, 2024), provisions 37 (malus and clawback) and 38 (disclosure) ; Directive (EU) 2017/828 (SRD II), art. 9a (remuneration policy)
